who stumbled immediately when Moses, their shepherd, departed from them. But look, I am leaving Xanthippus the deacon with you in my place.
He too proclaims Jesus Christ just as I do. For I too am a human being, like any one of you.
I do not possess the wealth that some people have, which ultimately destroys the person who acquires it. For it is of no use when he leaves it
in the earth from which he came, while the offenses and sins he acquired because of it remain with him. For only a few are both wealthy and merciful.
Nor do I possess this human beauty, in which all who trust are soon put to shame.
But if someone who possesses beauty becomes corrupt, his beauty does not help him at all. Instead, those who loved him for his beauty
will shun him all the more. For all the adornments of this world are loved at one time and hated at another.
But let your hope be in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and hold fast to us and regard us as servants of God.
And we too, unless we take on the burden of being worthy of this name, receive punishment, and it brings judgment and retribution upon us. And he prayed a long prayer with them.
He entrusted them to our Lord and said, “Lord of all the ages, who look to him, and God of all souls, who hope in him,
who saves his people from error and frees from corruption and slavery those who have obeyed him and come to his place of refuge:
be with the flock of Xanthippus. Anoint his sheep with your oil of life, and heal them of their leprosy.
Protect them from wolves and predators, so that they do not snatch them from his hands.” He laid his hand on them and said to them, “May there be with you
the peace of Jesus, and may it also go with us.” The apostle went out to begin his journey. They all accompanied him, weeping, and implored him by his Lord
to remember them in his prayer and not forget them. When the apostle climbed up and sat in the commander’s carriage, all the brothers remained behind.
The commander came and said to the driver, “I pray that I may be worthy to sit beneath the feet of the Son of God, Jesus Christ,
and be his driver on this road, which many know, so that he may be my guide on that road which only a few travel.”
When he had traveled about a mile, Judas Thomas asked the commander to get up and sit beside him.
He gave the driver permission to sit in his place. As they traveled along the road, Judas was speaking with the commander.
But the animals were exhausted from being driven so hard.
They stopped and refused to move. The commander was very distressed and did not know what to do.
He considered running on foot to bring other animals, whatever he could find, or horses, because
he was short of time. When the apostle saw him, he said to him, “Do not be afraid or anxious.
Only believe in Jesus, as I told you, and you will see great wonders.”
The commander said to him, “I believe in him, that everything is in his power to do for anyone who asks him.”
Judas saw a herd of wild asses grazing over there, away from the road, and said to the commander,
“If you believe in Jesus, go to the herd and say to them, ‘Judas, the apostle of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, says:
Let four of you come, for I need them.’” The commander went, very afraid, because there were so many of them.
And [?] as he went, they were coming toward him. When he came near them, he said to them, “Judas Thomas, the apostle of Jesus Christ,
says, ‘Let four of you come to me, because I need them.’” When they heard these words,
those wild asses came running swiftly toward him. When they reached him, they bowed before him through the providence of our Lord.
Judas Thomas, the apostle of our Lord, raised his voice in praise and said, “Praised are you, God of truth and Lord of all natures, for you
yourself willed by your own will and made all your works. You completed all your creatures and brought them into the order of their natures. You placed the fear of you upon them all.
that they might submit to your command. Your will itself opened a path from your hiddenness into the open and became the provider for every soul you made.
It was spoken through the mouths of all the prophets, in all visions, assemblies, and songs. But Israel was not persuaded, because of their evil inclination.
And you, because you are Lord of all and care for creation, spread your mercy over us through this one who came by your will and clothed himself in a body, your creation,
which you willed and formed according to your glorious wisdom. You ordered him in your hiddenness and established him in your revelation.
You gave him the name Son. He is your will, the power of your thought. You have distinct names: Father, Son, and Spirit,
for the care of your creatures and the nurturing of all natures. And you are one in glory [?], power, and will.
You are distinct without being divided, and one while remaining distinct. Everything stands in you and is not subjected [?].
For everything is yours. And I put my trust in you, my Lord. By your command I have brought this speechless animal into submission, so that you may provide for us and for them,
because there is need, and so that your name may be glorified through us and through the animal that has no speech.” When he had said these things, he said to those wild donkeys, “Peace be with you.
Because you have obeyed the word that rules over all, let four of you come and be harnessed in place of these animals that have stopped and cannot walk.”
Each of those wild donkeys crowded forward, vying over which of them would be harnessed. Now there were some there that were stronger than their companions.
These were harnessed, while the rest went behind and ahead of the apostle. After they had traveled a little way, he said to them,
“I am speaking to you, inhabitants of the wilderness. Stop and go to your pasture. For if I had needed all of you,
you would all have come. But now go back to the place where you were.” Those wild donkeys went away quietly,
until they were out of his sight. And the wild donkeys [?] gently and quietly, little by little, so that God's apostle would not be shaken.
When they reached the city gate, they turned aside and went and stood before the gate of that commander's courtyard.
Then that commander was astonished and said, “I cannot speak and recount what has happened.
Let another miracle take place, and then I will tell it.” The whole city was coming out, because they had seen those wild donkeys harnessed to the carriage,
and also because they had heard the report about the apostle who had gone there. The apostle said to that commander, “Where is your house?
And where are you taking us?” The commander said to him, “You know that you are standing at your servant's gate.
And these animals that came with you at your command know better than I do.” When the commander had said this, he jumped down from the carriage.
The apostle began to say, “Jesus, who is denied recognition in this place; Jesus, whose renown is foreign
in this city; Jesus, a stranger among these people; Jesus, who goes ahead of his apostle to every place and every city,
and through him is glorified and made known to all who are worthy of him; Jesus, who clothed himself in a body, became human, and appeared to us all, so that we would not depart from his love;
our Lord, who gave his life for us and purchased it with his blood, and acquired us for himself as a possession bought at a high price.
For what do we have to give him in exchange for his life? For he gave his life for us—not something that each person possesses.
Nor does he ask anything of us except that we ask him and live. While he was saying these things, many people were coming from every
place to see the new apostle of God who had come there. And Judas said, “Why are we standing idle?
Jesus, what is your will? Command the time, and let the deed be done.” Meanwhile, those demons intensified their attacks on the woman and her daughter,
and the members of that commander's household did not think they would survive. For the demons did not allow them to taste anything.
Instead, they had thrown them onto a bed, where they recognized no one, until the day the apostle came there.
The apostle said to one of the wild donkeys harnessed on the right, “Go into the courtyard, and as you stand there,
call those demons and say to them, ‘Judas the apostle, the disciple of Jesus Christ, says: Come outside here,
because I was sent on account of you and your kind, to drive you away to your own place. For the time of the end is approaching,
and you are going to your pit.’” That wild donkey went in, accompanied by a crowd of people, and said, “To you I speak, enemies of humanity.
To you I speak, you who shut your eyes against the light so that you will not see. For an evil nature cannot dwell in goodness. To you
I speak, offspring of Gehenna and destruction, children of the one who has not ceased to this day,
who keeps renewing the evil deeds that suit his nature. To you I speak, shameless ones, who destroy yourselves with your own hands.
What can I say about your end? I do not know. What can I recount? I cannot do it. For these things are too many to tell, and there is no end to them.
For however many your bodies may be, they are too few for your punishments. For I speak to you, demon, and to your son who does not follow [?].
For now I have been sent here against you. Why should I say more about your nature? For you yourselves know it better than I do,
and yet you act shamelessly. But now Judas Thomas, the apostle of Jesus Christ, who has been sent here in mercy and compassion, says:
Come out to this crowd standing here, and tell me what race you belong to.” At that very moment, the woman and her daughter came out,
looking like dead women, exposed and dishonored. When the apostle saw them, he was grieved for them and said, “No mercy was shown to you.
That is why you do not know how to show mercy either. But in the name of Jesus Christ, leave them and stand beside them.” While the apostle was saying
these words, the women fell down and died. For there was no breath in them, nor did they make any sound.
That demon cried out loudly and said, “You have come again, rebuker of our nature! You have come here again, destroyer of our race! You have come here again, you who erase our tracks!
As I see it, you do not want to leave us on earth. But you cannot do this to us at this time.” And Judas realized
that this was the demon he had driven out of that woman. And it said to him, “But I beg you, allow me to go and live wherever you wish.
I will accept your command, and I will not fear the one who has authority over me. For just as you have come to help, so I have come to destroy.”
And just as you receive blame if you do not fulfill the will of the one who sent you, so do I.
If I do not do the will of the one who sent me, I meet our common fate before my time. And just as your Lord helps you in what you do,
my father also supports me in what I do. And just as he prepares for you vessels [?] worthy for him to dwell in,
so he also gathers [?] for me vessels that obey him, so that I may carry out his will in them. And just as he feeds and provides for you
and those who obey you, so he also roasts and torments me and those in whom I dwell.
And just as he gives you the reward for your labor, namely eternal life, so he also gives me the recompense for my deeds: eternal destruction.
And just as you find rest in your prayer and your good deeds, in the Eucharist, in praises, in psalms, and in hymns about him,
so I too find rest in murder, adultery, sacrifices, and the pouring out of wine over burnt offerings.
And just as you turn people toward eternal life, so I too turn people toward myself, toward destruction and eternal torment.
You receive your reward, and I receive mine. And when that demon had said these things,
the apostle said, “Jesus says through me to you and your son: Do not enter any human settlement again. Instead, go and live outside every human settlement.”
Those demons said to him, “Look, we are going, as you commanded us. But what will you do to those who are hidden from you,
and [?] delight in them more than in you—those whom many worship, doing their will by sacrificing to them,
pouring out wine to them, and presenting offerings to them?” The apostle said, “They too will perish in the end, together with those who worship them.”
They searched for those demons, but they were not found. The women were lying speechless, like dead women. Those wild donkeys were also standing
beside one another, and they did not move away from one another. But the one that had been given speech through the power of our Lord
was standing apart from its companions. While all the people were silent and watching him to see what the apostle would do,
that wild donkey looked at them all and said to Judas, “Why are you standing idle, apostle of the Most High?
Look, the Advocate stands waiting for you to ask him, so that he may give to you. Why do you hesitate, good disciple?
Look, your Master wishes to show great things through your hands. Why do you stand there, herald of the Hidden One? Look, your Master wishes to reveal his hidden nature through your hands
to those worthy of him, so that they may hear these things. Why are you silent, you who do great things in your Lord’s name? Look, your Lord stands encouraging you not to be afraid.
For he does not abandon you, nor does his divinity allow your humanity to become distressed. Begin [?] to call on him, and he will answer you, as he always does. Why
does amazement seize you at his many deeds? These things he has shown through your hands are small. And if you were to recount the abundance of his gifts,
you could not recount them all. Why do you marvel at these bodily healings of his, which pass away,
when you remember his healing of those who belong to him, which does not pass away? Why do you ponder this temporary life, when every day you reflect on eternal life?”
But I say to you, the crowds who are standing here and waiting to see these women who lie here rise:
Believe the teacher of truth. Believe the one who shows what is true. Believe the revealer of hidden things. Believe the proclaimer of [?].
Believe the apostle of the chosen Son, Jesus Christ, who was born so that those who are born might live through his birth.
He was brought up so that complete upbringing might be seen in him. He entered the school so that perfect wisdom might be made known in him.
He taught his teacher, because he was the teacher of truth and the master of the wise. He went to the temple and presented an offering,
so that they might see that all offerings are sanctified through him. This is his apostle. This is the apostle of truth. This is the one who does the will of the one who sent him.
But a time will come when false apostles and lying prophets will come, whose end will be in keeping with their deeds. They are the ones who tell you,
“Guard yourselves against sins,” while they themselves speak sinful things all the time. They are the ones who wear sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves.
They are the ones who do not lawfully marry even one woman, yet through their words and deeds corrupt many women.
They are the ones who father no children, yet corrupt many children and bring disgrace upon them.
They are the ones who are distressed by the comfort of others and find comfort in their distress. They are the ones who are not satisfied with what they possess,
but desire that everything should serve them. They boast of these things and are regarded as disciples of Christ.
They are the ones with one thing in their mouths and another in their hearts. They are the ones who teach you to guard yourselves against evil things,
while they themselves do not do even one good thing. They are the ones in whose eyes adultery, theft, oppression, and greed are hateful,
yet all these things are secretly practiced among them, while they teach that no one should do them.” When he had said these things,
all the [?] were looking at him. When he fell silent, Judas said, “What should I think about your work, Jesus?
I do not know how to speak of you. O kind one, silent, gentle, and speaking, who sees what is in the heart and probes what is in the mind!
Glory to you, merciful one! Glory to you, living Word! Glory to you, hidden one of many forms! Glory to your mercies,
which have overflowed upon us! Glory to your grace, which has come upon us! Glory to your greatness, which became small for our sake! Glory to your exaltedness, which humbled itself for our sake!
Glory to your strength, which became weak for our sake! Glory to your divinity, which clothed itself in our humanity for our sake!
Glory to your humanity, which was made new for our sake! You died to give us life. Glory to your resurrection from the dead,
which became resurrection and revival for us! Glory to your ascent into heaven, through which you opened a path for us to the heights,
and you promised and swore to us that we would sit on the right and on the left and be judges with you. You are the Word of heaven.
You are the hidden light of the mind and the self-denial of the way of truth, the pursuer of darkness and the overthrower of error.” When the apostle had said these things,
he came and stood over those women who were lying there and said, “My Lord and my God, Jesus Christ, I have no doubt about you.
But I call on you, since you always help us, support us, and encourage us. He gives confidence and joy to his servant and apostle.
Let these women be healed and rise, and let them be as they were
before they were struck by the demons. When he said these things, those women recovered and sat up, well again.
Judas instructed that commander to have his servants take them inside and give them something to eat.
For they had tasted nothing for many days. When they had taken them inside, he said to those wild donkeys,
“Come after me.” They followed him until he had led them outside the gate. When they had gone outside, he said to them,
“Go in peace to your own land.” Those wild donkeys went away calmly, while the apostle stood watching them,
lest anyone hurt them, until they had gone far from his sight and he could no longer see them.
[The seventh act is finished.]
Eighth Act [Again, the eighth act.] Judas turned back from them and went to that commander’s house,
with a large crowd accompanying him. Now it happened that a woman, the wife of a relative of the king, whose name
was Mygdonia, had come to see the new spectacle of the new God who was being proclaimed, and the new apostle who had come to their country.
She was sitting in a chair, and her servants were carrying her. Because of the great crush of people,
they could not bring her in to him. She sent word to her husband, and he sent her his officers. They went ahead of her, pushing the people aside.
The apostle saw them and said to them, “Why are you pushing aside those who have come to hear the word?
You even try to make them move away, while you yourselves want to come to me, though you are very far away.
For our Lord used to say to the crowds who came to him, ‘You have ears, but you do not hear,
and you have eyes, but you do not see. Come to me, all you who are weary and carrying burdens, and I will give you rest.’”
He looked at those men and said, “Now the blessing that was given to them was meant for you who carry her.
For you are the ones carrying heavy burdens, and she controls you by her command. Although God
made you human beings, other human beings load you with excessive burdens as though you were animals.
Those who are carried on you think in their minds that you are not human beings like themselves.
They do not know that all human beings are equal before God, whether they are slaves or free.
God’s judgment, which is coming upon every soul on earth, is just, and no one escapes it:
neither slaves nor free people, neither rich nor poor. Nor will anything benefit those who have possessions.
Nor does the poverty of those in need exempt them from this judgment. For we were not commanded to do anything beyond our ability.
Nor were we commanded to carry heavy burdens, or to build buildings that carpenters construct with skill,
or to carry loads of hewn stones, whose stonecutters know their craft, but rather to do what we can:
to guard ourselves against adultery, the source of all evils, and against murder, because of which the curse came upon Cain,
and against theft, which brought Judas Iscariot to hanging, and against self-indulgence, which deprived Esau of his birthright,
and against greed, for whoever falls into it does not consider what he is doing, and against empty boasting and destructive slander, and against
evil actions, shameful deeds, hateful intercourse, and an impure bed, in which there is eternal condemnation.
It is this that forcibly leads the lofty away, casts them into the lowest depth, and brings them under its power,
so that they do not consider what they are doing, and their deeds are hidden from themselves. But listen to me, and conduct yourselves in chastity,
for this is preferred before God above all good things, and in asceticism, for this reveals communion with God
and gives eternal life and despises death. Conduct yourselves also in humility, for this was weighed against everything,
and it prevailed, won, and took the crown. And conduct yourselves with kindness, extending a hand to the poor and supplying what the needy lack.
Above all, you ought to conduct yourselves in chastity, for this is preferred before God, and this leads into eternal life.
For this is the foremost of all good things, and through it all good deeds are accomplished.
For whoever does not practice chastity cannot do anything good. For all good things follow after this chastity.
For chastity was revealed by God. It destroyed the Evil One. Chastity pleased God. For this reason [?]. Chastity
is an athlete who cannot be defeated. Chastity is truth that does not waver. Chastity is a tower that does not fall.
Chastity was worthy to be God's companion in conversation. Chastity itself is beauty when it is found among many.
Chastity overthrew corruption. Chastity is an envoy of peace, bringing good news of peace. Asceticism, for the person who acquires it,
frees him from everyday anxiety. Asceticism worries about nothing except how it can please its Lord.
Asceticism hangs on hope as it awaits salvation. Asceticism always sits in stillness, because it does nothing hateful.
Asceticism seeks a life of rest. It is a joy to everyone who calls upon it, and it exalts those close to it. Humility has subdued death
and brought it under its authority. Humility has overcome enmity. Humility is a gentle yoke that does not weary those who bear it.
Humility fears nothing and acts defiantly against nothing. Humility is peace and harmony, joy and rest.
Acquire chastity, take up asceticism for yourselves, and reach out toward humility. For in these three chief things it takes shape.
This Christ whom I proclaim. For holiness is God's temple, and whoever preserves it preserves his temple,
and Christ dwells in him. Self-denial is God's resting place. For our Lord fasted forty days and forty nights and tasted nothing.
Whoever observes it has Christ dwelling in him. For humility is a mighty strength. Our Lord said to Simon the apostle, “Put your sword back in its place.
If I wish to ask my Father for an army, he will give me more than twelve legions of angels.”
While Judas was saying these things, all the crowds were listening together and jostling one another.
The wife of Charisius, a relative of King Misdaeus, sprang up, came out of that chair, and fell to the ground at the apostle's feet.
She pleaded with him, saying, “I beg you, disciple of the new God who has come to a land barren of human habitation—
for we live in a wilderness, since we conduct ourselves like animals without reason, but now, through you, we are being brought to peace—
turn to me too and pray for me, so that I too may receive mercy from this God whom you proclaim and become a member of his household.
May I too join you in prayer, hope, and thanksgiving, and may I too receive the seal.
May I too become a holy temple, and may he dwell in me.” The apostle said, “I pray and ask you, my brothers in our Lord and my sisters in Christ,
that the word of Christ may settle in all of you and dwell in you, for you have authority over your own souls.” Then he began to say to the woman,
“Mygdonia, get up from the ground. Think of your soul, and do not concern yourself with your adornment, which passes away, or with the beauty of your body, which wears out, or with your clothes,
or with fame and authority in this passing world. Do not lower yourself to this filthy union
and so deprive yourself of that true fellowship. For adornment comes to nothing, beauty grows old and decays, and clothes wear out.
Authority passes away, with punishment for the way each person has exercised it. Union with it passes away amid great contempt.
Jesus alone endures, together with those who have hoped in him, taken refuge in him, and entrusted their souls to him.”
After saying these things, he said to the woman, “Go in peace, and may our Lord make you worthy of his divine mysteries.”
She said to him, “I am afraid to leave, lest you abandon me and move away to another place.” The apostle said to her,
“Jesus will not abandon you, because of his mercy.” She bowed down and worshiped him, because she thought he was Jesus.
She went home rejoicing. Meanwhile, Charisius, the relative of King Misdaeus, bathed and came up to eat dinner. He was asking
where his wife was, because she had not come out of the bedroom to meet him. Her maidservants told him that she was unwell. He entered the bedroom
and saw her lying on the bed with her face covered. He kissed her and said to her, “What is the matter today? You are distressed and angry.”
She said to him, “I am very tired.” He said to her, “Why did you not conduct yourself in a manner befitting your status as a free woman and stay at home,
rather than go and listen to idle words and acts of sorcery? But get up, come out, and have dinner with me.”
“For I cannot eat supper without you.” Mygdonia said to him, “Today I ask to be excused from supper with you and from your sleeping beside me,
for I am sweating very much.” When Charisius heard Mygdonia say this to him, he did not want to go out to his dining couch to eat supper.
Instead, he ordered his household to bring him food so that he could eat supper in her presence. They brought it in and set it before him.
He asked her to eat supper, but she would not. Since she would not eat supper, he ate alone.
Charisius said to her, “For your sake I asked to be excused from my lord King Mazdai and from the supper, yet you were unwilling to eat supper
with me.” Mygdonia said to him, “Because I have no appetite.” He got up to go upstairs and sleep, as was his custom.
She said to him, “Did I not tell you plainly that today I ask to sleep alone?” When he heard these words,
he went away and slept in another bed. When he awoke from sleep, he said to her, “My lady and my sister Mygdonia, listen to the dream I had tonight.
I dreamed that I was reclining before my lord King Mazdai, with a table set before us. I saw an eagle coming down from heaven.
It took a pair of partridges from before me and King Mazdai, carried them up to its nest, and put them there. Then it came back and flew above us.
King Mazdai ordered a bow to be brought to him. That eagle came again and took a dove and a turtledove from before us.
Mazdai shot an arrow at it. The arrow passed through it from one side to the other but did not hurt it. Instead, it flew away to its nest. I awoke trembling,
distressed over that partridge I had tasted, because it would not let me put any more of it into my mouth. Its taste is still in my mouth!” Mygdonia said to him,
“Your dream is good. You eat partridges every day, but perhaps that eagle had never tasted a partridge until now.”
At dawn Charisius, King Mazdai’s relative, got up early and dressed. He put his left shoe on his right foot and said
to Mygdonia, “What is this happening? First the dream, and now this!” Mygdonia said to him,
“This too is not bad but good. From another bad occurrence, a good one comes.” He washed his hands
and went to greet King Mazdai. Mygdonia, Charisius’s wife, also went early to greet Judas the apostle.
She found him sitting and speaking with the commander and a large crowd. He said to them, “My children,
that woman who received our Lord into her heart and soul yesterday—whose wife is she?” The commander said to him,
“She is the wife of Charisius, King Mazdai’s relative. Her husband is a harsh man, and whatever he asks of the king, the king grants his wish.
He will not allow her to remain as she has promised. For even before the king he speaks very highly of her beauty and says that there is no one like her.
She too loves him very much, and these things you speak of are foreign to them.”
Judas said, “If our Lord has truly shone into her soul and she has received the seed sown in her, she will have no regard for this temporary life
and will not fear death. Nor will Charisius himself be able to do anything more to her or cause her suffering, because greater than he is the one who
which she had received in her soul, whether she had received it steadfastly in perfect love. When Mygdonia heard these things, she said to Judas:
“Truly, my lord, through your prayer I have received the living seed of the word, and through my Lord Jesus I am bearing fruit like the seed.”
Judas said, “Our souls, which belong to you, thank you, our Lord. Our spirits, which are truly your possession, thank you, my Lord.
“These bodies of ours thank you, my Lord, because you have made them worthy to become a dwelling place for your Spirit, who is forever glorified.”
The apostle said to all those who were there, “Blessed are the holy ones whose souls have never despised them, because they have gained them
“and have no doubts about them. Blessed are the spirits of the holy ones who have received the crown and come up from the contest to what was entrusted to them.
“Blessed are the bodies of the holy ones, which have been found worthy to become pure temples for Christ to dwell in.
“Blessed are you, holy ones, for you have the authority to ask and receive. Blessed are you, holy ones, for you have been called judges.
“Blessed are you, holy ones, for you have been given authority to forgive sins. Blessed are you, holy ones, for you have not lost what was entrusted to you,
“but joyfully carry it up with you to the heights. Blessed are you, humble ones, whom God has made worthy
“to inherit the kingdom. Blessed are you, humble ones, for you are the ones who have conquered the evil one.
“Blessed are you, humble ones, for you are children of the light. Blessed are you, humble ones, for you will see the face of your Lord.
“Blessed are you, ascetics, for you will find rest and delight in these spiritual things that neither pass away nor perish, and those who eat them do not hunger.
“Blessed are you, ascetics, for you have been delivered from sin.” While the apostle was saying these things, all the crowds were listening to him.
Mygdonia, the wife of Charisius, the friend of King Misdaeus, was becoming increasingly steadfast in holiness
and ascetic discipline and complete humility. All day long they delighted in the praises and greatness of the Lord.
Charisius, the friend of King Misdaeus, came for the meal and did not find his wife at home. He began asking everyone in his household about her:
“Where has your mistress gone?” One of them told him, “She went to that foreigner, and she is there.”

When he heard this from a member of his household, he became angry with the rest of his household because they had not told him what had happened. He went and bathed and came up while it was still light.
He sat waiting for Mygdonia to come. When evening came, she arrived. He met her and said to her,
“Where have you been until now?” She told him, “I had gone to the physician’s house.” He said, “Is that foreign sorcerer a physician?”
She told him, “Yes, he is a physician, and he is different from all other physicians. For all physicians heal these bodies that perish,
“but this physician heals bodies together with souls, which will no longer perish.” When Charisius, the relative of King Misdaeus, heard these things,
he was inwardly angry with Mygdonia and with that foreigner. But he said nothing to her, because he was afraid of her.
For she far surpassed him in wealth and also in understanding. He went in to the dining couch and [?] to eat supper.
She went back into her outer bedroom. He told his servants to call her to come out and have supper with him, but she was unwilling.
When he heard that she was unwilling to come out, he went in to her and said, “Why do you not want to come out and have supper with me?
Perhaps you do not even want to sleep beside me as you usually do. This is what frightens me so much, especially since I have heard that this sorcerer and deceiver
has taken it upon himself to keep a man from being with his wife. What nature commands and the gods themselves approve,
he forbids.” While Charisius was saying these things to her, Mygdonia remained silent. He spoke to her again:
“My sister, my lady, my beloved, my companion Mygdonia, do not be led astray by empty, foolish words,
or by the acts of sorcery you have heard that he performs in the name of his god. For since the day the world came into being,
it has never been heard that anyone brought a dead person to life. Yet this man, as I hear, supposedly makes a show of bringing the dead to life. And they also say that he neither eats nor drinks.
But that is because he owns nothing. For what can someone eat who does not even have bread for the day? And he wears just one garment because he has no other.
He takes no payment from anyone because he knows that he does not truly heal anyone.” While Charisius was saying these things to Mygdonia,
she remained silent as a stone, praying and asking when dawn would come and when she could go and see the apostle of God. Then he left her
and went to have supper, troubled, but thinking that he would sleep beside her as usual. The moment he left her, she knelt down
and prayed, saying, “My Lord and my God, Christ who gives me life, give me strength to overcome the shamelessness of Charisius.
Grant me to preserve the chastity in which you delight, and through which I find eternal life.”
After praying, she covered her face and lay down. As soon as Charisius had finished supper, he came in and stood over her. He was taking off
his clothes when she noticed him and said to him, “You have no place beside me, because my Lord Jesus, with whom I have been united, is greater than you,
and he is beside me at all times.” Charisius laughed and said to her, “You have certainly been well caught by that sorcerer!
And you have made a fine mockery of him who said, ‘You will not live before God unless you remain chaste.’” Having said this,
he brazenly tried to lie down beside her. But she would not tolerate it. She cried out bitterly against him and said, “I appeal to you, O new God,
who came to India through a foreign man! I appeal to you, my Lord Jesus: do not abandon me, for I have taken refuge in you.
For I have heard that you yourself sought those who did not know you. Now I am asking you, since I have just heard of your goodness and have believed in you:
come to my aid and rescue me from the shamelessness of Charisius. Do not let his uncleanness overpower me, and do not let him have a place beside me.”
She got up, bound his hands, and fled from him. She wrapped herself in the curtain that hung over the bedroom doorway,
covered herself, and went out to the woman who had raised her. She slept beside her that night.
But Charisius was in anguish all night, striking his hands together. He wanted to go out during the night.
He would inform King Misdaeus about the violence done to him. And he was thinking and saying:
“If I go to King Misdaeus in the great distress I am in, who will bring me into his presence? For I know that if fortune had not overthrown me
and cast me down from my pride and arrogance, from greatness into lowly insignificance, and had not separated my beloved Mygdonia from me,
even if King Misdaeus were standing at my door at this moment, I would not go out and answer him. But I will wait until dawn.
I know that whatever I tell King Misdaeus, he will do what I want. I will tell him about that stranger’s sorcery:
how he has acted violently and [?] the exalted into the depths. For it is not my separation from companionship with Mygdonia that grieves me.
Rather, I grieve for her herself, because her greatness has been diminished, her noble status has fallen, and her lofty soul has been humbled.
A woman whom no one in her household had ever seen in any indecent state was running naked out of her bedroom.
I do not know where she went. Perhaps she went out into the street under the spell of that stranger’s sorcery.
I do not know where she went, for nothing could be seen with her.” When he had said these things, he began to weep and say, “Alas for you, my true companion!
I have been deprived of you so suddenly! Alas for you, my beloved, who loved me! You were dearer to me than all my family. Nor did I have a son or daughter by you in whom I could find comfort.
You had not spent a whole year with me before the evil eye took you away from me. If only the violence of death had taken you from me!
Then I would have counted myself among kings, rulers, and nobles—and not a foreign man, who is perhaps a slave who has run away from his masters and come here because of my bad fortune.
I will have neither rest nor respite until I destroy him, bring punishment upon his head, and take my revenge on him.
Tonight I will not appear before King Misdaeus. And if he does not do what I want and does not bring punishment upon that stranger’s head—
I will also speak to him about Siphor, the commander, because he was the cause of this ruin. For there he is, living in his house,
and many people come and go to see him. He teaches them a new teaching about chastity. He teaches and says
that no one can live unless he gives up everything he has and becomes destitute and a beggar like him. Now he is seeking to make companions for himself.”
While Charisius was thinking these things, dawn broke. He got up early, dressed, and put on his shoes. He wore shabby clothes, his face looked dreadful, and he was deeply dejected.
He went in to greet King Misdaeus. As soon as King Misdaeus saw him, he said to him, “Why is it that in this
dejected state you have come to me? Why do you look so gloomy, and why is your face so changed?” Charisius said to him:
“King Misdaeus, I have a new affair to tell you about, and a new calamity that Siphor has brought here. A Hebrew magician is living in his house
and does not leave him. Many people come to him, and he teaches them a new god and establishes new laws,
such as we have never heard before. He says, ‘You cannot become children of the eternal life that I teach
unless you separate yourselves, each man from his wife and each woman from her husband.’ Now it happened that my wretched, miserable wife went to see him and heard his words.
She believed them, got up in the night, and fled from me—she who could not endure being away from me for a single hour, and who could not bear to be without me [?].
But send for Siphor and that sorcerer who is staying with him, and punish them. Otherwise all the people of our country will perish through his words.
When Mazdai heard these things from his relative Charisius, he said to him, “Do not be distressed or grieve. I will send for him, bring him here, and punish him.
You have [?] your wife. For if I avenge others who cannot avenge themselves, will I not avenge you even
more?” He ordered that Siphor the commander be summoned to him. They went to his house and found him sitting at the right hand of Judas, the apostle of God.
Mygdonia was sitting at his feet with a large crowd, listening to him. Those who had gone to fetch Siphor the commander spoke and said to him,
“You are sitting here listening to empty words, while King Mazdai, in his anger, wants to destroy you because of this sorcerer and deceiver whom you have brought into your house!”
When Siphor the commander heard this, he was distressed—not because the king was threatening him, but because the king had heard that he was acquainted with Judas the apostle.
Siphor said to Judas, “It is on your account that I am distressed. For I told you a day ago
that this woman is the wife of Charisius, a relative of King Mazdai, and he will not allow her to do what she promised.
Whatever he says to the king, the king does as he wishes.” Judas said to Siphor, “Do not be afraid.
Instead, believe in Jesus, who gave up his spirit for me and for you, and for all those who have taken refuge in him and come into his place of shelter.”
When Siphor the commander heard this, he put on his clothes and went to King Mazdai. Meanwhile, Judas was asking Mygdonia what had caused
her husband to become angry and devise these things against them. She said to him, “It was because I did not give myself over to corruption with him.
For in the evening he wanted to subjugate me and throw me beneath the one he serves. But the one to whom I entrusted myself delivered me from his hands.
I fled naked from him and slept at my nurse’s house. I do not know what has happened to him, that he should plot these things against you.”
The apostle said to her, “These things do us no harm, my daughter [?]. But believe in Jesus, and he will restrain Charisius’s lust from you.
He will deliver you from corruption and filth, and he will be your guide on the fearsome road,
leading you to his own kingdom and his Father’s. He will bring you into everlasting joy [?] and give you a kingdom that neither passes away nor changes.”
When Siphor stood before King Mazdai, Mazdai questioned him, saying, “What is the news about him, and where did it originate?
What does that sorcerer who is staying with you teach?” Siphor said to him, “Surely you know, my lord, that I and all my friends have suffered great sorrow over my wife,
whom, as you know, many hold in honor, and over my daughter. Everything I possess counts as nothing to me compared with them.
What a time of suffering and what a trial came upon them! They had become an object of ridicule and a curse throughout the whole country.
But I heard the report about this man, went to him, pleaded with him, and brought him along. We came
here. As I traveled with him on the road, I saw extraordinary wonders. Here too, many saw and heard what that wild donkey said.”
Even the demon revealed who he was. He healed my wife and my daughter, and now they are well. He asked for no payment except faith
and holiness, so that they might share in what he does. He says, “Fear the one God, the Lord of all, and Jesus Christ his Son,
and you will live forever and ever.” He eats nothing except bread and salt, from evening to evening, and drinks water.
He prays a great deal, and whatever he asks of God, God gives him. He also instructs us that this God of his is holy, good, kind,
gentle, and life-giving. “For this reason,” he says, “those who believe in him approach him in purity, holiness, and love.”
When King Mazdai heard these things from Siphor, he sent many soldiers from his presence to the house of Siphor, the commander,
to bring Judas Thomas and anyone they found with him. When they went inside, they found him sitting and teaching a large crowd.
Mygdonia too was sitting at his feet. They were afraid when they saw the large crowd surrounding him, and they went to tell King Mazdai,
“We did not dare say anything to him, because there was a large crowd with him. Mygdonia too
is sitting at his feet and listening to his words.” When Mazdai and Charisius heard this, Charisius sprang up from before King Mazdai.
He took a large number of soldiers with him and said, “I will go and bring him, and Mygdonia too, whose mind he has taken away.”
He hurried to the house of Siphor, the commander, and when he arrived, he found Judas sitting and teaching.
When he entered, he saw Judas, but he did not find Mygdonia there, for she had gone home.
For she knew that they were telling her husband that she was there. Charisius said to Judas,
“Get up, you wicked man, corrupter, and enemy! What can your sorcery do to me? I will turn your spells back upon your own head.”
When he said this to him, Judas looked at him and said, “May your threats return upon you! You cannot harm me at all,
because my Lord Jesus Christ, in whom I take refuge, is greater than you, your king, and all your forces.” Charisius took a cloak belonging to one of his household
and threw it around Judas’s neck, saying, “Drag him away! Let me see whether Jesus will rescue him from my hands.” They dragged him along
until they reached King Mazdai. When Judas stood before King Mazdai, the king said to him, “Tell me about yourself,
and by whose power you do these deeds.” But Judas remained silent and gave him no answer.
Mazdai gave orders to the soldiers, and they struck him a hundred and twenty blows. He ordered them to take him to prison in bonds.
They bound him and took him away. When he went and entered the prison, they bound him and took him away.
When he went and entered the prison, Mazdai and Charisius were considering how to kill him, because all the people
were worshiping him as a god. They were seeking grounds to say that he insulted the king and was a sorcerer. But Judas, as he went to prison,
was glad and rejoiced, saying, “I thank you, my Lord Jesus Christ.”
For you have made me worthy not only to believe in you, but also to endure many things for your sake. And he said, “I thank you, my Lord, that you have made me worthy of these things.
I thank you, my Lord, that your care was over [?], and you made me worthy to endure many hardships for your sake. I thank you, my Lord,
that for your sake I have become a sorcerer, an outcast, a poor man, and a beggar. Therefore I shall receive a share in the blessedness of the poor and in the rest of the weary,
and in the blessedness of those whom people hate, persecute, and insult, and against whom they speak
hateful words. Look, for your sake I am hated and separated from many people. For your sake they say things about me of which I know nothing.”
While he was praying, everyone in the prison watched him praying.
They asked him to pray for them too. When he had prayed and sat down, Judas began to recite this hymn.
Hymn of Judas Thomas. Hymn of Judas Thomas, the apostle in the land of the Indians.
When I was a little child and lived in my kingdom, in my father’s house, I rested amid the wealth and splendor of those who raised me.
From the East, our homeland, my parents equipped me and sent me out. From the wealth of our treasury they generously tied up a load for me. It was large, yet light,
so that I could carry it alone. It was gold from Beth Ellaye, silver from great Ganzak, rubies from India, and agates from Beth Kashan.
They equipped me with adamant, which crushes iron. They took off the splendid robe they had made for me in their love, and my purple toga,
woven and measured to fit my stature. They made an agreement with me and wrote it on my heart so that it would not be forgotten:
“If you go down into Egypt and bring back the one pearl that lies in the midst of the sea, near the hissing serpent, you shall put on
your splendid robe and your toga that rests upon it, and with your brother, our second in rank, you shall be an heir in our kingdom.” I set out from the East and went down,
with two escorts beside me, for the road was dangerous and difficult, and I was a child traveling it. I crossed the borders of Mesene,
the gathering place of the merchants of the East. I reached the land of Babylon and entered the walls of Sarbug. I went down into Egypt,
and my companions parted from me. I went straight toward the serpent and lodged near its dwelling, waiting for it to doze and fall asleep,
so that I could take my pearl from it. Since I was alone, I was solitary; I was a stranger to those with whom I lodged.
[?] a man of my own race, a freeborn son of the anointed. He came and joined me, and I made him my intimate friend, a companion with whom I shared my business.
I warned him against the Egyptians and against associating with the unclean. I dressed as they dressed, so that they would not suspect that I had come from outside
to take the pearl, and would not stir up the serpent against me. But somehow they realized that I was not their countryman.
They dealt with me deceitfully and even gave me their food to eat. I forgot that I was a king’s son and served their king.
I forgot the pearl for which my parents had sent me, and under the weight of their stupor I fell into a deep sleep. And all these things
that had happened to me my parents perceived, and they grieved for me. A proclamation was made in our kingdom that everyone should hasten to our gate: the kings and chiefs of Parthia.
And all the nobles of the East bound me with a pledge that I would not be left in Egypt. And they wrote me a letter.
And every noble put his name in it: “From your father, the King of Kings, and your mother, the ruler of the East, and from your brother, our second in rank,
to you, our son in Egypt: peace. Awake and rise from your sleep, and hear the words of our letter. Remember that you are a king’s son.
Look at the slavery you have endured and whom you have served. Remember the pearl for which you were sent to Egypt. Remember your splendid robe,
and remember your glorious mantle, which you are to wear as your adornment. Your name has been entered in the book of the valiant, and with your brother, [?], you will be in our kingdom.”
My letter was a letter that the king sealed with his right hand, to protect it from the wicked people of Babylon and the fierce demons of Sarbug.
It flew and settled beside me and became entirely speech. At its voice and the sound of its stirring, I awoke and rose from my sleep.
I took it and kissed it, opened it, and read it. The words of my letter corresponded to what was inscribed on my heart.
I remembered that I was a king’s son, and my freeborn nature demanded its own. I remembered the pearl for which I had been sent to Egypt.
And I began to cast a spell on the terrible, hissing serpent. I made it drowsy and put it to sleep by invoking my father’s name over it,
and the name of our second in rank, and of my mother, the queen of the East. I snatched the pearl and turned to go back to my father’s house.
I stripped off their filthy, unclean clothing and left it in their country. I directed my journey toward the light of the East, our homeland.
I found my letter, which had awakened me, ahead of me on the road. Just as it had awakened me with its voice, so now it shed its light on me.
Wrapped in silk [?], it shone before me with its appearance. With its voice and its guidance, it again encouraged me to hurry,
and drew me onward with its love. I went out and passed through Sarbug. I left Babylon on my left and reached great Mesene, the merchants’ harbor,
which lies beside the sea. My splendid robe, which I had taken off, and my mantle, which was wrapped around it, my parents sent there from the heights of Hyrcania,
through their treasurers, who were entrusted with it because of their faithfulness. I did not remember its appearance, since I had left it in my childhood
in my father’s house. Suddenly, when I faced it, the garment seemed to me like a mirror of myself. I saw it entirely in my whole self, and I too encountered my whole self in it.
For we were two, distinct from one another, yet we were also one in a single likeness. I also saw that the treasurers who had brought it to me were likewise
two, yet of one likeness, for the single mark of the king was inscribed on them. Through their hands, his hands restored to me what had been entrusted to them and my wealth:
my splendid robe, adorned with glorious colors, with gold and beryls, carbuncles and agates, and sardonyxes of varied colors.
It was also fashioned in its full length, and all its seams were set with diamonds. The complete image of the King of Kings was depicted and portrayed all over it.
Sapphire stones were also interspersed among its colors. And I saw that movements of knowledge were stirring throughout it, and that, as though to speak,
it was preparing itself. I heard the sound of its songs, which it uttered as it descended [?]: “I am the one diligent in deeds,
for whom they raised me in my father’s presence.” And I too perceived within myself that my stature was growing in keeping with his labors. And with its royal movements,
It spread out toward me in its entirety, and in the hands of those bringing it, it hurried toward me so that I might take it. Love also urged me to run to meet it
and receive it. I stretched out and received it. I adorned myself with the beauty of its colors, and wrapped my brilliantly colored robe entirely around myself.
I put it on and went up to the gate of greeting and worship. I bowed my head and worshiped him—the radiance of my father, who had sent it to me—because I had carried out his commands.
He too did what he had promised. At the gate of his satraps I mingled with his nobles, for he rejoiced in me and received me, and I was with him in his kingdom.
And with the sound of [?], all his servants praise him. And I will hasten onward, and with my offering and my pearl I will appear with him before our king.
Here ends the hymn of Judas Thomas the apostle, which he spoke in prison.
Song of Praise of Thomas the Apostle. Again, a song of praise of Thomas the apostle.
Praised are you, Father, Lord of all, the ineffable Being, hidden from all worlds in the radiance of your glory. Exalted are you, Son, firstborn of life,
who comes from the exalted Father and is the Word of life. Praised are you, the one Father, who portrays himself in wisdom in all creatures and in all worlds.
Exalted are you, Son of light, wisdom and power and knowledge, who are in all worlds. Praised are you, God Most High,
who shone forth from his concealment into the open through all his prophets. Exalted are you, Son of mercy, in whom
they were all perfected in wisdom and silence. Praised are you, majestic Father, who begot his firstborn in silence and stillness of thought. Exalted are you, worshiped Son,
who shone forth from the Father in his form, in stillness and praise. Praised are you, good Father, who revealed the mystery of his firstborn to his prophets through the Holy Spirit.
Exalted are you, chosen Son, who revealed the Father's glory to his apostles in all [?]. Praised are you, pure Father,

who sanctifies his greatness forever through his firstborn, who gives life to the pure one; who sanctifies his greatness forever through his firstborn, who gives life to his creation. Exalted are you, beautiful Son,
who shone forth from the Father's radiance and redeemed our souls with his innocent blood. Praised are you, Father, ruler of all, who dwells in his majestic light,
hidden in his glory and revealed to all through his grace. Exalted are you, Son who brings all to perfection, who is sown [?] in the living earth.
Before the ages you exist in your holy Father. Praised are you, God who nourishes all, who are in all worlds, in the height and in the depth,
and there is no place empty of you. Exalted are you, Son, worshiped fruit, who shone upon all in mercy, put on our humanity, and killed our enemy.
Praised are you, boundless God, who made his angels from the outpourings of his Spirit, and his servants from his burning fire.
Exalted are you, Son of light, who rides on the wind, wrapped in the Father's light, upon the holy clouds.
Praised are you, Father who gives life to all, who gathers the worlds to his glory through his Beloved, so that they may offer him praise. Exalted are you, Son of life,
for the Father satisfies the holy ones with his gift, and they journeyed from him and arrived on his path of peace. Praised are you, God who gives life to all,
who revealed the mysteries of his Son through the Spirit to his holy ones, in stillness and rest. Exalted are you, Son, fruit of the Father,
who shelters his chosen ones beneath his wings, fulfilled his Father's will, and redeemed his beloved ones. Praised are you, good Father.
He gives life to all creation through his Beloved, in mercy and grace, through the death of his crucifixion. Praised are you, firstborn Son.
He nourishes the worlds with his body and wipes away our sins with the sign of his wounds and with his blood sprinkled upon us. Glorified are you, good Father.
He dwells in the pure heart, in the understanding of his worshipers. He is hidden from everyone's sight, yet revealed himself to us in his Christ. Praised are you, Son, the Word.
He proclaims his coming in silence and put on our humanity, and redeemed us through his living and pure blood. Glorified are you, living Father.
You brought our dead condition to life when we had strayed from your path. We were dead and lost, and your mercy came upon us.

Praised are you, beloved Son. You brought our dead condition to life and turned us back from our wandering. You became for us the medicine of life through your life-giving body and the sprinkling of your living blood.
Glorified are you, exalted Father, by all our mouths and all our tongues. You were reconciled to us through your Christ, and we tasted you through your fruit,
and became children of your peace. Praised are you, Son, maker of peace. You healed our wounds and soothed our distress, and gathered together
our wandering minds. You led us in your truth, and through you we came to know your Father. Glorified are you, Father, ruler of all. You sent us your living and life-giving fruit,
and through the blood of his cross he reconciled your mercy with your creatures. Praised are you, Son, Word of light.
You shone forth from on high and satisfied us with the knowledge of you. You cleansed our uncleanness and brought our dead condition to life through your sign, the cross of light.
Glorified are you, Father of all praises, and exalted is your great name through all ages. You did not exact our debts from us, but gave us life through your Christ, [?] of your will.
Praised are you, Son, voice filled with understanding, our holy priest. You made atonement for us through your pure and holy offering, and poured out your living blood on behalf of sinners.
Glorified are you, exalted Father. You were hidden from all the ages, and revealed yourself as you willed to all your worshipers. Praised are you, Son of life,

who fulfills the Father's will. You brought peace to your creatures so that through you they might worship the one who sent you and share in your mysteries. Glorified are you, Father, higher than all. Every knee
will bow to you, both in heaven and on earth, through your Beloved. Praised are you, worshipful Son of perfect mercy.
Through him peace and hope came upon creatures, so that they might know the Creator. Glorified are you, Father, giver of life to all. The wealth
of your mercy does not run out through the abundance of your gifts, and at all times you yourself feel the need to give to us. Praised are you, Son, the fruit.
You are the gate of light and the way of truth. You led us in your footsteps so that we might reach the house of your exalted Father.
Glorified are you, gracious Father. You brought us peace through our giver of life, and revealed to us your glorious and holy mysteries through the hearing of his teaching.
Praised are you, Son, the Father's only Son. Your mercy came upon us, and you marked us with your living and life-giving cross.
All our mouths and all our tongues glorify the Father, worship the Son, and praise your Holy Spirit, as do the worlds and creatures, hidden and visible.
Your angels glorify you on high through Christ, who became peace and hope in Sheol for the dead who came to life and were raised.
We ask you, our Lord and giver of life: in your grace, fulfill for us everything you have said and promised, and bring us into the place of your peace. For you are our giver of life.
You are our Advocate. You are the medicine of our life. You are our victorious standard. Blessed are we, my Lord, because we have known you. Blessed are you, in whom we have believed.
Blessed are we through your wounds and your blood shed for us. Blessed are we because you are our great hope. Blessed are we because you are our God, forever and ever. Amen.
Now Charisius, Mygdonia’s husband, was going home very happily, because he thought to himself that from now on his wife would be with him
as she had been before, before she heard the message of Judas and believed in our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God. When Charisius arrived,
he found his wife sitting there, her face scratched and her clothes torn. She looked like a madwoman because of Judas.
He said to her, “My lady and my sister Mygdonia, what is this terrible frenzy that has seized you? Why have you done these things? I am Charisius, the husband of your youth.
I have authority over you from the gods and from the law. Why have you now behaved like a madwoman? Why have you made yourself a laughingstock throughout this whole country?
But now put the thought of that sorcerer out of your mind. For I will remove him from your sight, so that you will never see him again.”
When she heard these things from her husband Charisius, she became still more distressed and agitated.
Again he said to her, “What offense have I committed against the gods, that they have brought me to this great suffering? What sin have I committed before them,
that they have brought me to this humiliation and ridicule? I beg you, Mygdonia, do not choke the life out of me by the sight of you, and do not
hurt your heart with your brooding. I am Charisius, the husband of your youth. I am your true husband,
whom the whole country honors and fears. I do not know what to do now, or how to conduct myself.
What else am I to think? Shall I remember your beauty in my heart and remain silent? Or shall I recall your lovely ways and say nothing?
Who has a fine and beautiful treasure taken from him and lets go of it? Or can I endure losing the lovely charms you have always shown me?
Your sweet fragrance is still in my nostrils, and your beautiful complexion is before my eyes. My life is being taken from me, and my seeing eye,
with which I used to see—they are outrageously taking it from me. My right arm is being cut off from me. My beauty is being destroyed,
and my comfort is being made a source of distress to me. My joy has turned to sorrow, and my rest has become anguish.
My life is being exchanged for death, and my light is being dyed with darkness. Let the members of my large family not look upon me,
because they have given me no help in this anguish. Let my distinguished friends not look upon me, because they have not rescued me from this anguish.
I will no longer worship the gods of the East, who have brought these misfortunes upon me. I will not pray before them or sacrifice
to them again, nor will I present an offering to them, because I have been deprived of this true companionship. For what should I pray to them for now? What should I ask of them anymore?
Or what should I ask them to give me, when they have deprived me of the woman who was more precious to me than everything I possessed in the world, and in whom I found rest?
For I have wealth beyond my ability to manage, and possessions beyond my ability to count. I have also been made a ruler,
and I am called second to the king. Many fear me, and many are under my authority.
But who would take from me all my splendor and my great wealth, and give me one hour of your former years, Mygdonia?”
Who, then, blinded one of my eyes? Yet your own eyes used to look at me as usual.
Who, then, cut off my right arm? Yet I embraced you with my left arm.” Charisius was saying these things and weeping.
Mygdonia sat like a [?] and did not look at him, but at the ground, and remained silent.
He approached her again and said to her, “My daughter and my beloved Mygdonia, remember that out of all the women of India
you were the one who pleased me, and I chose you, although I could have married many women who were better than you.
But I am not lying, Mygdonia. No, by God, there is no other woman for me in all India who is like you. What
beauty, what care, what charm, and what fine ways I am losing! Alas for me forever, for I no longer hear you speak.
Even if only to insult me, [?]. I beg you, lift your eyes and look at me, for I am far better than that sorcerer.
I am more handsome than he is, and I have wealth and honor. Everyone knows that no one has a lineage like mine.
You yourself are more precious to me than my family and everything I possess, yet now they are taking you away from me.” While Charisius was saying these things,
Mygdonia said to him, “Charisius, the one I love is better than everything you have acquired
and everything you possess. For everything you possess comes from the earth and remains on the earth. But the one I love is in heaven,
and he takes me up to heaven to be with him. Your wealth passes away, your beauty decays, and your clothes wear out, pass away, and perish.
You are left alone with your offenses and sins. Unless you are freed from them, they accompany you. Do not remind us of your former worldly deeds,
which I pray and ask my Lord to wipe away for me. Do not remind me of your filthy, impure pleasures and your bodily acts,
from which, in my love for my Lord, I pray to be freed. I have forgotten them all. Your habits
and your intimacies and your deeds perish with you. But my Lord and Savior Jesus alone remains forever,
as do the souls that take refuge in him. The one in whom I have taken refuge and believed—
he saves me and rescues me from all your shameful deeds, which I used to perform with you when I was not a believer.”
When Charisius heard these things, he went and lay down in distress. He said to her, “Think this over and consider it in your mind all night tonight.
If you will be with me as you were before you saw that sorcerer’s face, I will do whatever you wish.
And if you wish, because of the love you have for him, I will bring him out and send him away, and he can go to another country.
I will not cause you distress, for I know that you are deeply attached to him. This did not begin with you;
rather, something like this has happened to many women. And this was the outcome: they remembered themselves and considered what had happened to them,
and they came to their senses and were freed from disgrace and ridicule. So do not let these things I have told you seem to you [?].
as nothing. Do not let outsiders come to you, and do not make me an object of shame, ridicule, and gossip among [?]. And when he had said these things to her,
he went to sleep. But Mygdonia took ten silver coins and went to the prison without anyone noticing her,
to give them to the prison guards so that they would let her in to Judas. And as she was going, Judas met her
as he was coming to her. When she saw him, she was afraid, for she thought he was one of the officials,
because of the great light that went before him. She said, “Woe to you, my weak soul, for you are lost!
I will never again see Judas, the apostle of Jesus, the living God, because I have not yet received the seal from him.”
She fled and went into another street, saying, “It would be better for me to be caught by other, poorer men, whom I could persuade,
rather than be caught by this great man, who will not accept a bribe from me.” While Mygdonia was thinking these things,
Judas came and went in after her. She was afraid and fell down in her fear. He stood over her and said to her,
“Do not be afraid, Mygdonia. Jesus Christ will not abandon you. Your Lord, to whom you have entrusted your soul, will not abandon you.
The merciful one, whose compassion is abundant, will not abandon you. The kind one will not abandon you, because of his kindness. The good one will not abandon you, because of his goodness.
The great one will not abandon you, because of his greatness. Get up from the ground above which you once stood.
Look at the light of your Lord, who does not leave those who love him to walk in darkness. See the companion of his servants,
who becomes their light in the darkness. See the helper of his servants, who becomes their help in afflictions.”
Mygdonia got up, looked at him, and said to him, “Where were you going, my lord? And who brought you out of prison,
outside to see the sun?” Judas said to her, “Our Lord Jesus Christ is mightier than all powers, kings, and authorities.
He opened the doors and put the guards to sleep.” Mygdonia said to him, “Give me the seal of Jesus Christ, and let me receive his gift from your hands
before you depart from this world.” She took him along, went home, and entered her courtyard. She woke her nurse and said to her, “My mother and nurse, Narcia,
all the help you have given me and all the comforts you have provided from my childhood until now—you have done them for me [?], and my gratitude
to you for them lasts only a short time. But do me this kindness, which lasts forever, and you will be repaid by the one who gives everything to his own
and does not take [?] away from them.” Narcia said to her, “What do you want, my daughter Mygdonia? And what comfort do you have,
that you promised to give me all those earlier honors? For the foreign man has not left you, and you have made me an object of shame in this place.
Now, then, what new thing do you want to do to me?” She said to her, “Be my companion in everlasting life,
and let me receive from you the care that brings me to completion. Secretly take a loaf of bread for me, and bring me a cup of mixed wine. Have pity on
my freedom.” Narcia said to her, “I will bring you plenty of bread and many quarter-measures of wine.” To Narcia, her nurse.
“I have no need of many [?], but only a cup of mixed wine, one whole loaf, and a little oil. Bring it to me even if it is in a lamp.”
When Narcia brought it to her, Mygdonia uncovered her head. She stood before the holy apostle, and he took the oil
and poured it on her head, saying, “Holy anointing oil, given to us for anointing, and hidden mystery of the cross revealed in it,
you are the one who straightens bent limbs. You are our Lord Jesus, life, healing, and forgiveness of sins. May your power come and rest upon this oil,
and may your holiness dwell in it.” He poured it on Mygdonia’s head and said, “Heal her of her former scars,
wash away her wounds, and strengthen her in her weakness.” When he had poured the oil on her head, he told her nurse to anoint her
and wrap a linen cloth around her waist. There was a pool belonging to their water conduit, and Judas went up and stood above it.
He baptized Mygdonia in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. When she came up and dressed, he brought and broke the Eucharistic bread, and brought the cup.
He gave Mygdonia a share in the table of Christ and in the cup of the Son of God. He said to her, “From now on,
you have received the seal and have gained life for ever and ever.” A voice was heard from heaven saying,
“Yes, amen and amen.” When Narcia heard this voice, she was amazed. She too asked the apostle
that she might also receive the seal. He gave it to her and said, “May the grace of Jesus be with you, as it is with the rest of your companions.”
He went back to prison and found the doors open and the guards asleep. Judas said,
“Who is like you, God, who withholds his love and mercy from no one? Who resembles you in mercy and compassion,
except your Father, who delivered his worlds from distress and error? Love that conquered desire, truth that abolished falsehood,
beautiful one in whom no ugliness is seen, humble one who overthrew pride, living one who abolished death, and rest that put an end to weariness!
Glory to the Only Begotten who is from the Father! Glory to the mercy sent forth from mercy! Glory to your mercy shown to us!” When he had said these things,
the guards awoke and found all the doors open and the prisoners asleep. They said,
“We forgot these doors and did not shut them. For if an enemy had done this, no one would have remained here.”
Charisius rose early in the morning and went to Mygdonia and her nurse. He found her and her nurse
praying and saying, “New God, who came here through a foreign man; holy God, hidden from all the people of India;
God who showed us his glory through his apostle Thomas; God whose fame we heard and in whom we believed; God who, because we realized that he has life,
is the one to whom we run so that we may live; God who, because of his mercy and compassion, reached down to our lowliness;
God whom we sought when we did not know him; God who dwells on high, from whom nothing in the depths is hidden: you, my Lord, remove Charisius’s burning lust from us.
You, my Lord, shut his lying mouth, and cast him beneath the feet of your faithful.” When Charisius heard these things,
He said to Mygdonia, “You were right to call me evil, diseased, hateful, and bitter. For if I had not done your will,
this evil and bitterness would not have surrounded me, nor would you have called on that man’s sorcery against me. But what have you decided, Mygdonia?
What do you want me to do for you? Believe me, Mygdonia: that sorcerer is of no use, and he does not do anything he promises anyone.
But I will show you with your own eyes everything I tell you, if you will be persuaded by me, listen to my words, and behave toward me as you used to behave
toward me.” He approached her again and pleaded with her, saying,
“I will not grow weary if you will listen to me. Remember, my sister, your wedding day and the first day on which you received me. Now tell me truthfully:
who is better for you—me at that time, or Jesus now?” Mygdonia said to him, “Charisius, that time demanded its due and came to an end.
This time also demands its due. That was a time of beginning; this is a time of completion. That was a time of temporary life that passes away;
this is a time of eternal life. That was a time of joy that passes away; this is a time of everlasting joy that does not pass away.
That was a time of day and night; this is a time of day without night. You saw how that wedding feast passed away and came to an end.
But this wedding feast will never pass away. That was a wedding feast of corruption; this is a wedding feast of eternal life.
Those were groomsmen and bridesmaids who pass away; these are faithful groomsmen and bridesmaids who remain forever.
That stands on the dust, where there is turmoil; this stands on a passage of fire on which grace has been sprinkled.
That is a bridal chamber that is dismantled; this is a bridal chamber that lasts forever. That was a bed covered with fine clothes that wore out; this is
a bed covered with love and true faith. You are a bridegroom who passes away and is replaced; Jesus is the true bridegroom who remains forever,
and never again dies or decays, [?] who bestows life that never passes away.” When Charisius heard these things,
he went and told King Misdaeus. King Misdaeus said, “Let us bring him here and put him to death.” His friend Charisius said to him,
“Be patient with him a little. Bring him out, make things bitter for him, and frighten him. Perhaps he will go and persuade Mygdonia
to behave toward me as she used to.” King Misdaeus sent for Judas Thomas, the apostle of the Most High, and had him brought.
All those prisoners were distressed because Judas the apostle had gone away from them.
They longed for him and said, “They have taken away from us even the comfort we had.” King Misdaeus said to Judas,
“Why do you teach a doctrine that gods and human beings hate, and in which there is nothing good?” Judas said to him,
“What evil am I teaching?” Misdaeus said to him, “You say that human beings do not live with God
unless they keep themselves pure for the God whom you proclaim.” Judas said to him, “Indeed, that is what I say, and I am not lying
in what I say. Can your servants stand before you in shabby clothing, or when they are filthy or repulsive?
You, then, who are an earthly king and will decay in the earth, have demanded good and pure things from your servants.
For this reason, you who are an earthly king and will decay in the earth have demanded good and pure things from your servants.
[?] my king, how can you say that I speak wrongly when I say that his servants should serve him in holiness, purity, and self-denial?
They should be free from worry and distress, and keep away from the excessive burden of sons and daughters,
and from excessive concern about wealth, and from the turmoil and vanity of possessions. For those who serve you, without being your slaves,
you have wished to conduct themselves according to your ways. And if one of them transgresses one of your commands, they receive punishment from you.
How much more, then, ought we who have believed in the name of this God of mine to serve him in purity, holiness, self-denial, and integrity,
and chastity! And let all these bodily things be foreign to us: adultery, theft, drunkenness, debauchery, and service to the belly,
and shameful deeds and hateful actions.” When King Mazdai heard these things, he said to Judas, “Look, I am releasing you.
Go and persuade Mygdonia, the wife of Charisius, not to separate from him.” Judas said to him,
“If you wish to do anything to me, do not delay. For if she has truly accepted what she has heard,
neither iron nor fire nor anything harsher than these can do anything to her or cut off the one who holds her soul.”
King Mazdai said to Judas, “I have heard that spells undo spells, and that an antidote undoes the bite of a viper—
an antidote made from another creature more dangerous than the viper. Now, then, if you wish, you can undo your spells,
those earlier ones, and establish peace and harmony between the man and his wife, and spare your own life.
For you have not yet had your fill of life. But know that if you do not persuade her, this life that everyone holds dear—
I will deprive you of it.” Judas said to him, “This life is borrowed, and this present time passes away and changes.
But the life that I teach about never passes away or changes. And this beauty and youth that are now visible
will soon no longer be mine.” King Mazdai said to him, “I have advised you about what will help you. But you know better than I do.”
When Judas Thomas went out from the presence of King Mazdai, Charisius came to him and said to him, “I beg
you: I have never wronged you in anything, or anyone else, or the gods.
Why have you brought this calamity upon me, and why have you brought this destruction into my house? What benefit do you gain from this?
Tell me, and I will bring it to you without delay. Why do you treat me so hatefully? You will not escape from my hands.
For know that if you do not persuade her, I will destroy you. And I will also deprive her of this life.
And finally I will destroy myself, taking myself out of the world. And finally I will destroy myself, taking myself out of the world.”
And if, as you say, there are life and death—and if, as you say, there are life and death, and condemnation and acquittal, and judgment and repayment—
there I will stand with you in judgment [?]. And if your God, whom you teach about, is just and calls people to account justly,
